processing: Fresh leaf is spread out, fixed, rolled, then piled and smothered before a first drying, followed by pan-firing and a final drying. The smothered pile is what yellows the leaf and the liquor.
harvest_season: Picked at one bud with one opened leaf up to one bud with two leaves just opening. Like other bud teas of Zhejiang, it is normally a spring tea.
appearance_dry: Tight, fine strands, slender as lotus seed hearts, with plenty of visible down.
appearance_wet: Tender yellow leaf sets that hold together in small clusters.
taste_profile: Little is recorded about its flavour beyond praise for its fragrance. As is typical of lightly smothered yellow teas, expect a mellow, gently sweet cup with less sharpness than a Zhejiang green.

brewing.notes: General settings for young, downy leaf rather than a documented house rule. The down will cloud the first cup slightly; cooler water keeps it soft.

vintage_note: As usual for Chinese bud-style yellow teas, it is sold as the current spring's harvest and is best drunk within about a year. It has no ageing tradition, and it is a small regional tea, so ask for the harvest year and the place on the mountain.
description:
Mogan Huangya is a yellow tea from Moganshan in Deqing county, northern Zhejiang, a province far better known for its greens. It is described as the only yellow tea of the Huzhou area, and it was among Zhejiang's first group of province-level named teas.

The make resembles a green tea until the piling stage. After rolling, the leaf is heaped and smothered while still damp, then dried in stages with a spell in the pan. That smothering is the entire point: it turns the leaf and the liquor yellow and takes some of the edge off.

In the cup you get clear yellow-green liquor from fine, downy strands. Specific tasting notes are hard to come by, so treat it the way you would treat other yellow teas: expect something softer than Longjing or Anji Bai Cha, and brew with water below boiling so you do not scald the young leaf.

When buying, look for fine, even, hairy strands and a true yellow tint. A bright green leaf and a sharp grassy smell suggest a green tea sold under the name, or one with too little smothering.
history:
Tea on Moganshan is traditionally traced to monks who built hermitages and planted bushes on the mountain in the Jin dynasty, an account worth taking as local tradition rather than a firm record.

The modern tea has clearer dates. In the spring of 1956 the tea scientist Zhuang Wanfang, resting at Moganshan, bought tea from an old woman selling it in the street and was struck by how good it smelled. In 1979 the yellow tea was created with the involvement of Zhang Tangheng and Zhuang Wanfang of the tea department at Zhejiang Agricultural University.
